issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: Kwame, a 68-year-old African-American dancer, survived a near-fatal motor-vehicle collision when a delivery truck clipped the back of his car on a rainy evening. The impact jolted his body into a violent motion, leaving him shaken, his spine cracking, and the world turning sideways. When the ambulance arrived, he watched the paramedics hurriedly lift him onto a stretcher while the driver, a city official, apologized, yet Kwame felt that the people who were supposed to protect him had let him fall. He began to question whether his own body was a reliable ally and whether the institutions meant to safeguard citizens were trustworthy. The experience planted a seed of self-doubt, a conviction that his body could betray him again, and a belief that those in charge had failed him. From that moment, Kwame's doubts crystallized into concrete avoidance. He no longer left his apartment; the streets seemed full of unseen hazards. He refused to attend the community dance classes he had led for decades, shunning any social contact with former classmates or dancers. Even the routine of attending counseling sessions became a battleground-he would refuse to talk about the accident or revisit the imagery that surfaced, as if thinking of it could summon the danger back into his life. He had come to believe that any discussion of the crash might trigger the same physiological alarms, making the therapy rooms feel as perilous as the street corners of his youth. The belief that he could not trust his own body amplified a heightened sense of threat. Kwame found that a single sound-the sudden clatter of a loose kitchen cabinet-could launch him into a state of hyper-vigilance, as if a vehicle could rear up from nowhere. He could not tolerate any delays; a five-minute wait at a bus stop felt like an imminent threat. He insisted on having a wall behind him whenever he was in a public space; the solidity of the surface seemed to offer a shield against an unseen onslaught. The persistent threat reinforced his earlier convictions that his body was unreliable and that the system that ought to protect him had let him down. The cycle tightened: the more he felt unsafe, the more he avoided leaving, and the more he felt the world as a potential threat. The fragmented memory of the crash-an incomplete picture punctuated by flashes of smoke and screeching metal-spurred Kwame's avoidance. He could not piece together a coherent narrative of what happened, which made him fearful of any moment that might force the story to resurface. When he tried to recall the event, he found the details slipping away like sand. The absence of a clear story fed his self-doubt and reinforced his sense that the institutions that had been supposed to guide him through the aftermath were inadequate. The broken memory also made him feel that his body had betrayed him; the missing pieces of the accident felt like gaps where danger had slipped through the cracks. In turn, his fear of confronting these incomplete recollections pushed him further into isolation. The relentless sense of threat, rooted in those incomplete memories, triggered additional avoidance. Kwame refused to enter the same grocery store he once frequented, fearing that a sudden noise could unleash an attack on him. He stayed inside his apartment, letting the quiet become a comfort and the silence a shield. Even the gentle hum of the refrigerator became a potential cue for danger. The avoidance, in turn, kept him in confined spaces where his fear of loud sounds and unexpected delays grew, reinforcing the original sense of threat. Today, Kwame stands at the threshold of a counseling office, his palms clammy on the door handle. He has finally decided to seek help, perhaps because the cumulative weight of isolation has begun to affect his sleep and his once-vibrant dance routine. His greatest fear is that the cycle of doubt, threat, and avoidance will drag him into a state of complete withdrawal from his community and from the movement that defined him. He hopes that by confronting the fragmented memory and the lingering belief that his body and institutions are unreliable, he can loosen the grip of the threat that has kept him immobilized for years.
